title: Lesson 4 - A1.2.3 Sabotage
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How can digital systems be sabotaged and what are the consequences?

sections.heading: What is sabotage?
sections.text: Sabotage is the deliberate act of damaging, disrupting or interfering with data, systems, devices or infrastructure to cause harm or stop them working properly.
points: Example: a hacker injects false data into a company's AI system, so it makes wrong decisions, causing financial loss or system failure
Targets: commercial, government and individuals, and it can be an act of terrorism
On a computer or network it can mean changing settings without authorisation or uploading malware
In extreme cases: destroying a company's property, or even violence
Online, libelling or doxxing a person or company can also be seen as sabotage
Damage can spread beyond the organisation to anyone whose devices link to it

sections.heading: The four types of data sabotage

head: Type
What happens
Effect
rows: Data tampering
Data is deliberately altered to cause damage
A service or website stops working properly or shows wrong or inappropriate content
Data poisoning
Errors or false data are deliberately added to an AI system's training data
The AI becomes biased and makes errors
Data destruction
Files are deleted or overwritten. Nothing is altered, it is simply removed
Systems stop running; catastrophic for users, especially if personal or financial data is lost
Deepfakes
Video, audio, images or documents are digitally manipulated or made by AI
Mistrust, reputational damage and financial loss

sections.heading: Data tampering
sections.text: Deliberately altering data to cause damage. A service or website may stop working as expected, or show content that is wrong or inappropriate.
points: Tampering can also be unintentional, e.g. human error that deletes or changes critical data, but that is NOT classed as sabotage
Link to Lesson 3: front-end tampering changes what the public sees; back-end tampering changes databases

sections.heading: Data poisoning
sections.text: AI systems are built by analysing huge amounts of training data. For example, an AI that makes music is trained on examples of instruments and melodies.
points: Data poisoning is deliberately altering, or adding errors to, training data
This causes bias and errors in the AI system
Your slides call it the digital version of the Luddites, who smashed machines they saw as a threat

sections.heading: Deepfakes and fakes
sections.text: A deepfake is a digitally manipulated video that changes or misrepresents an original, e.g. changing someone's face, voice or words to give a new meaning. The term now includes videos made with AI, and fakes can be audio, images or documents too.
points: Used to cause mistrust, reputational damage or financial loss
Can trick employees into giving scammers access to company data or money
Can make a business or its staff look bad, and fake media is easy to make and share
As AI improves, fakes get harder to verify, so even internet-savvy people share fakes thinking they are real
Example: in 2023 a fake image of Pope Francis in a Balenciaga puffer jacket got over 20 million views
Tip from the slides: AI often struggles to draw human hands, which can give a fake away

sections.heading: Case study: artists fighting back
sections.text: Your slides link to an article about Nightshade, a tool artists use against AI image generators. Glaze hides an artist's style from AI; Nightshade 'poisons' images so AI trained on them learns the wrong things.
points: What impact do fake images have on society? Think: trust, misinformation, reputations
Why would artists want to stop their work being used to train AI? Think: copying their style without permission or payment
Are Nightshade and Glaze good or bad? Think: protecting artists vs it being data poisoning, the same technique used in sabotage

sections.heading: Damage to, or hijacking of, physical systems

head: Target
Examples
Why it's a risk
rows: Machinery and vehicles
Power generation equipment; autonomous devices such as self-driving cars, traffic lights and central heating
Can be damaged or taken over by individuals, groups or terrorist organisations
Internet of Things (IoT) devices
Door locks, alarm systems, baby monitors, cameras
Security is often weak, and each device is another way into a home network. Door locks can be disabled remotely
Industrial processes
Chemical plants, factories, food distribution
One weak link in a supply chain exposes the whole chain: tampered food safety data, counterfeit products, production delays, financial crises
Critical infrastructure
National: water, energy, communication, transport. Commercial: distribution of products and services, often linked to online shopping
An attack can cripple whole cities, so governments use top-level security to prevent terrorism

sections.heading: Why critical infrastructure matters most
points: Attacking one device affects one user. Attacking critical infrastructure affects whole cities
These are essential services: water, power, communication and transport keep people safe and healthy
Other services depend on them, e.g. hospitals need power and water
That's why it's the answer to the Flying Start question on which sabotage has the biggest impact on society

keyIdea: Sabotage is deliberate damage or disruption. It can target data (tampering, poisoning, destruction, deepfakes) or physical systems (machinery, IoT devices, industrial processes, critical infrastructure), and the bigger and more essential the target, the more people are harmed.
flashcards: Sabotage
Deliberately damaging, disrupting or interfering with data, systems, devices or infrastructure to cause harm or stop them working.
Data tampering
Deliberately altering data to cause damage, so a service or website works wrongly or shows wrong content.
Unintentional tampering
Accidentally deleting or changing data through human error. Not classed as sabotage.
Training data
The large amount of example data an AI system learns from.
Data poisoning
Deliberately altering or adding errors to AI training data, causing bias and errors in the AI.
Bias (AI)
When an AI system makes unfair or skewed decisions because of faulty or poisoned training data.
Data destruction
Deleting or overwriting files so they're gone. Nothing is altered, just removed.
Deepfake
A digitally manipulated or AI-made video that changes someone's face, voice or words to give a new meaning.
Fakes
Manipulated audio, video, images or documents used to cause mistrust, reputational damage or financial loss.
Spotting AI images
AI often struggles to draw human hands, which can give a fake image away.
Doxxing
Publishing someone's private information online to cause them harm. Can be a form of sabotage.
Libel
Publishing false statements that damage someone's reputation. Online, it can be a form of sabotage.
Nightshade
A tool artists use to 'poison' their images so AI trained on them learns the wrong things.
Glaze
A tool that hides an artist's style from AI image generators.
Autonomous device
A device that runs itself, e.g. self-driving cars, traffic light systems, central heating.
Internet of Things (IoT)
Everyday devices connected to the internet, such as door locks, alarms and baby monitors.
Why IoT is risky
Security is often weak, and every device is another access point into a home network.
Industrial process sabotage
Attacks on chemical plants, factories or food distribution systems.
Supply chain risk
One weak link can expose the whole chain: tampered safety data, counterfeit goods, delays, financial crises.
Critical infrastructure
Essential services such as water, energy, communication and transport. Attacks can cripple whole cities.
Commercial infrastructure
Systems that distribute products and services, often linked to online shopping.
Luddites
People who smashed machines they saw as a threat. Data poisoning is called their digital version.

quiz.q: Which type of sabotage could have the biggest impact on society?
quiz.e: Critical infrastructure (water, energy, communication, transport) affects whole cities, not just one organisation.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a deepfake?
o: An AI-generated video showing a politician saying something they never said
quiz.e: A deepfake manipulates someone's face, voice or words, often using AI.

o: Destroying data so it cannot be recovered
Deliberately adding false or misleading data to a dataset
Encrypting data and demanding a ransom
quiz.e: Data poisoning corrupts AI training data so the AI becomes biased and makes errors.

o: Deliberately damaging or disrupting data, systems, devices or infrastructure
quiz.e: The key word is deliberate: sabotage is done on purpose to cause harm.

quiz.q: An employee accidentally deletes critical data. Is this sabotage?
o: Yes, all data loss is sabotage
quiz.e: Your slides say unintentional tampering is not classed as sabotage, because sabotage must be deliberate.

quiz.q: Hackers delete and overwrite a company's files without changing anything first. This is:
quiz.e: Data destruction removes or overwrites files. Nothing is altered, just wiped.

quiz.q: What happens to an AI system whose training data has been poisoned?
o: It becomes biased and makes errors
quiz.e: Poisoned training data leads to bias and errors in the AI's output.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a way deepfakes harm businesses?
o: Tricking staff into giving scammers money or data
Making it harder to know what's real
quiz.e: Deepfakes cause mistrust, reputational damage and financial loss. They don't back anything up.

quiz.q: According to your slides, what can often give away an AI-generated image?
o: It is always black and white
quiz.e: AI currently struggles to draw human hands, as the Pope image shows.

quiz.q: Why are IoT devices like baby monitors and door locks easy targets?
o: Their security is often weak and they add access points to a home network
They never connect to the internet
quiz.e: Weak security plus more access points makes IoT devices attractive to criminals.

quiz.q: A self-driving car is an example of:
quiz.e: Autonomous devices include self-driving cars, traffic light systems and central heating.

quiz.q: What can happen when one link in a food supply chain is attacked?
o: Only that one company is affected
The whole chain is exposed: tampered safety data, counterfeit products, delays
quiz.e: One vulnerable link can expose the whole supply chain to interference.

quiz.q: Which of these is national critical infrastructure?
quiz.e: Critical infrastructure includes water, energy, communication and transport.

quiz.q: Why is attacking critical infrastructure more serious than attacking a single device?
o: It can cripple whole cities and put many people's safety at risk
quiz.e: One device affects one user; infrastructure affects everyone who relies on that essential service.

quiz.q: Publishing someone's private information online to harm them is called:
quiz.e: Doxxing (and libel) can be seen as sabotage on the internet.

quiz.q: What does the tool Nightshade do?
o: Poisons images so AI trained on them learns the wrong things
quiz.e: Artists use it to protect their work, and it works by poisoning data, the same technique used in sabotage.

apply.title: Spot the sabotage
apply.intro: Read each situation and pick the type of sabotage or the best answer. In the exam, link your answer to the scenario.

items.task: A hacker changes the prices on an online shop so every product shows £0.01.
items.e: The data was deliberately altered so the site works wrongly: data tampering.

items.task: Someone feeds thousands of mislabelled photos into a company's AI system so it starts recognising cats as dogs.
items.e: Corrupting AI training data causes errors: data poisoning.

items.task: A hospital's patient records are wiped and overwritten, and the system won't start.
items.e: Files deleted or overwritten, not altered: data destruction.

items.task: A finance worker gets a video call from what looks and sounds like their boss, asking for an urgent £50,000 transfer. It wasn't really the boss.
items.e: AI-faked video and voice used to trick staff into handing over money is a deepfake.

items.task: A family's smart door lock is unlocked remotely by a criminal while they're on holiday.
items.e: Internet-connected door locks often have weak security and can be disabled remotely.

items.task: Hackers take control of a city's traffic light system and turn every light green.
items.e: Traffic light systems are autonomous devices that can be hijacked as an act of sabotage.

items.task: Food safety test results at a supplier are secretly changed, so unsafe food passes inspection.
o: Sabotage of an industrial process (supply chain)
items.e: Tampering with food safety and testing data is a named risk to food supply chains.

items.task: A national energy company is attacked, and power goes out across several cities.
items.e: Energy is critical infrastructure, and attacks can cripple whole cities.

items.task: A worker accidentally deletes a key spreadsheet while tidying up files. Is it sabotage?
items.e: Sabotage must be deliberate. Accidental deletion is human error.

items.task: A fake photo of a celebrity endorsing a scam product spreads online, and fans lose money.
items.e: Fake images cause mistrust, reputational damage and financial loss.

items.task: Someone posts a rival business owner's home address and phone number online to harass them.
items.e: Doxxing is listed on your slides as a form of online sabotage.

items.task: Which target would cause the MOST harm to society if sabotaged?
items.e: Water is critical infrastructure, so an attack affects whole populations.

pts: The deliberate act of damaging, disrupting or interfering with data, systems, devices or infrastructure
to cause harm or stop them working properly
exam.tip: Use the word "deliberate". It's what makes it sabotage rather than an accident.

pts: Deliberately altering data to cause damage
so a service or website doesn't work as expected, or shows wrong or inappropriate content
exam.tip: Definition + effect. Bonus understanding: accidental changes are human error, not sabotage.

exam.q: 3. Describe what is meant by data poisoning.
pts: Deliberately altering, or adding errors or false data to, the training data used by an AI system
which causes the AI to become biased and make errors
exam.tip: Mention AI training data. That's what makes it poisoning rather than general tampering.

exam.q: 4. Explain one difference between data tampering and data destruction.
pts: Data tampering changes (alters) the data so it is wrong
whereas data destruction deletes or overwrites the data so it is gone completely

exam.q: 5. Give one example of a deepfake and explain why it can be harmful.
pts: Example, e.g. an AI-generated video of a politician saying something they never said
Harm, e.g. people believe and share it, spreading misinformation and mistrust
Consequence, e.g. damages the person's or organisation's reputation, or tricks people into losing money
exam.tip: 1 mark for the example, then explain the harm AND what it leads to.

exam.q: 6. Explain why Internet of Things (IoT) devices in the home are a target for sabotage.
pts: Their security is often weak
so criminals can take control, e.g. disabling door locks, and each device is another access point into the home network
exam.tip: Point (weak security) + linked consequence (more ways in / devices hijacked).

exam.sc: Riverside Water supplies drinking water to 400,000 homes. Its treatment plant is run by internet-connected sensors and control systems. An AI system, trained on years of sensor data, predicts when pipes need repairing. Finance staff often approve payments after receiving voice messages or video calls from managers.
exam.q: 7. Explain how data poisoning could affect Riverside Water's AI system.
pts: An attacker deliberately adds false or wrong sensor data to the AI's training data
so the AI becomes biased and makes errors in its predictions
which means pipes that need repairing are missed (leaks, unsafe supply) or money is wasted on unneeded repairs
exam.tip: Cause → effect on the AI → effect on Riverside. Use the scenario's pipe repairs.

exam.sc: Riverside Water supplies drinking water to 400,000 homes. Its treatment plant is run by internet-connected sensors and control systems. An AI system, trained on years of sensor data, predicts when pipes need repairing. Finance staff often approve payments after receiving voice messages or video calls from managers.
exam.q: 8. Explain how a deepfake could be used to steal money from Riverside Water.
pts: A criminal creates a fake voice message or video call that looks and sounds like a manager
asking finance staff to approve an urgent payment
Because staff already approve payments this way, they are tricked and the money goes to the criminal
exam.tip: The scenario tells you staff approve payments from voice and video. That's the weakness to use.

exam.sc: Riverside Water supplies drinking water to 400,000 homes. Its treatment plant is run by internet-connected sensors and control systems. An AI system, trained on years of sensor data, predicts when pipes need repairing. Finance staff often approve payments after receiving voice messages or video calls from managers.
exam.q: 9. Explain why sabotaging Riverside Water is more serious than sabotaging a single device.
pts: Riverside Water is critical infrastructure
so an attack could affect 400,000 homes, not just one user
Water is an essential service
so unsafe or no water could put people's health at risk and disrupt other services such as hospitals
exam.tip: Two points with reasons. Use the numbers from the scenario (400,000 homes).

exam.sc: Riverside Water supplies drinking water to 400,000 homes. Its treatment plant is run by internet-connected sensors and control systems. An AI system, trained on years of sensor data, predicts when pipes need repairing. Finance staff often approve payments after receiving voice messages or video calls from managers.
exam.q: 10. Assess which form of sabotage poses the greatest risk to Riverside Water.
pts: Identifies a form of sabotage as the greatest risk, e.g. hijacking the internet-connected control systems
Explains how it could happen using the scenario (internet-connected sensors and controls)
Explains the impact: unsafe or no water for 400,000 homes, a risk to health and safety
Compares with another form, e.g. a deepfake payment scam causes financial loss but doesn't endanger the public
Considers a third form, e.g. data poisoning of the AI could cause failures more slowly and less obviously
Justified conclusion: the greatest risk is the one with the biggest impact on public safety, with a reason
exam.tip: Top-grade "assess" = compare at least two forms of sabotage, weigh likelihood AND impact, use the scenario, and give a clear judgement.
